title: Instructional Simplicity as a Learning Science Principle
author: Sol in the Wild
source: Sol in the Wild on Substack, February 7, 2026
summary: Sol argues that simplicity in instructional design is not a luxury but a cornerstone of learning science. Complex, multi-layered lessons—the kind that showcase a teacher's preparation and sophistication—often undermine the very learning they intend to support. When students are cognitively overloaded by complicated examples, multiple pathways, or too many steps, their working memory fills quickly and long-term learning suffers. Simplicity is not dumbing down; it is clarity. The most effective lessons isolate the learning target, remove extraneous cognitive load, and give students room to think. This principle appears across the evidence: from Rosenshine's principles of instruction to the success of direct instruction models to recent work on cognitive load theory. Sol shares classroom examples where deliberate simplification improved learning. A history teacher stopped using colorful multimedia-rich slides and returned to straightforward text and images; engagement and retention improved. A math teacher reduced the number of worked examples per lesson and increased spacing between problems; accuracy went up. The pattern is consistent: less is more. Instructional simplicity frees cognitive capacity for actual learning rather than burning it on processing visual novelty or navigating convoluted explanations. Teachers often resist this, associating simplicity with boringness, but evidence shows students learn more from clean, focused instruction than from flashy, complex presentations.
